'''Richard Ithamar Aaron''', {{Post-nominals|country=GBR|size=100%|FBA}} (6 November 1901 – 29 March 1987), was a [[Welsh people|Welsh]] philosopher who became an authority on the work of [[John Locke]]. He also wrote a [[Philosophy#Historical overview|history of philosophy]] in the [[Welsh language]].

==Early life and education==
Born in [[Seven Sisters, Wales|Blaendulais]], [[Glamorgan]], Aaron was the son of a Welsh [[Baptist]] [[draper]], William Aaron, and his wife, Margaret Griffith.<ref name="Jones">{{cite ODNB|doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/65645|title=Aaron, Richard Ithamar (1901–1987), philosopher|year=2004|last=Jones|first=O. R.}} [also accessible in {{Cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/oxforddictionary01matt |title=Oxford Dictionary of National Biography |year=2004 |volume=1 |pages= |url-access=registration |via=[[Internet Archive]]}}]</ref> He was educated at [[Ystalyfera]] Grammar School,<ref>{{Citation |title=Aaron, Richard Ithamar, (6 Nov. 1901–29 March 1987), Professor of Philosophy, University College of Wales, Aberystwyth, 1932–69 |date=2007-12-01 |work=Who Was Who |url=http://www.ukwhoswho.com/view/10.1093/ww/9780199540891.001.0001/ww-9780199540884-e-161308 |access-date=2025-02-12 |publisher=Oxford University Press |language=en |doi=10.1093/ww/9780199540884.013.u161308 |url-access=subscription}} [alternatively see: {{Citation |title=Who was who 1981-1990 |page=1 |year=1991 |url=https://archive.org/details/whowaswho19811990008unse |url-access=registration |via=Internet Archive}}.]</ref> then at the [[University of Wales]] from 1918, where he studied history and philosophy. In 1923 he was elected a Fellow of the university, allowing him to attend [[Oriel College, Oxford]], where he gained a DPhil in 1928 for a [[dissertation]] on "The History and Value of the Distinction between Intellect and Intuition".<ref name="BioDict20CPhil">{{Cite book |last1=Lewis |first1=Peter |title=Biographical Dictionary of Twentieth-Century Philosophers |publisher=[[Routledge]] |year=1996 |isbn=978-0-415-06043-1 |editor-last=Brown |editor-first=Stuart C. |location=London |page=1 |chapter=Aaaron, Richard Ithamar |editor-last2=Collinson |editor-first2=Diané |editor-last3=Wilkinson |editor-first3=Robert |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DfGIKKb3iZEC&pg=PA1}}</ref>

==Career==
In 1926 Aaron was appointed a lecturer in the Department of Philosophy at the [[University College of Swansea]].<ref name="BioDict20CPhil"/> After the retirement of W. Jenkyn Jones in 1932, Aaron was appointed to the chair of philosophy at [[University College of Wales, Aberystwyth]] where he settled, initially on the nearby hill of [[Rhos Bryn Hir|Bryn Hir]] and later at [[Garth Celyn]].{{Sfn|Jones|1988|p=377}}<ref name="Jones" />

Although his early publications focused on [[epistemology]] and the [[history of ideas]], Aaron became fascinated with the work and life of [[John Locke]]. The interest was sparked by his discovery of unexamined information in the Lovelace Collection: notes and drafts left by John Locke to his cousin [[Peter King, 1st Baron King|Peter King]]. There he found letters, notebooks, catalogues, and most pertinently, an early draft of Locke's "[[An Essay Concerning Human Understanding]]", hitherto presumed missing. Aaron's research led to the 1937 publication of a book on the life and work of Locke that subsequently became an accepted standard work.<ref name = Jones/> The proofs were read by Rhiannon Morgan, whom Aaron married in 1937. They had five children.<ref name = Jones/> One of their children is [[Welsh-language literature|Welsh literature]] specialist [[Jane Aaron (educator)|Jane Aaron]], born in 1951.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/whoswhoinworld200000unse |title=Who's who in the world 2005 |date=2004 |location=Chicago |publisher=Marquis Who's Who |others= |isbn=978-0-8379-1133-5 |url-access=registration |via=Internet Archive}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date= |title=Aaron, Jane 1951- |url=http://www.worldcat.org/identities/lccn-no2003-16419/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210902032330/http://www.worldcat.org/identities/lccn-no2003-16419/ |archive-date=2 September 2021 |access-date=11 March 2019 |website=[[WorldCat]] |publisher=[[OCLC]] |language=en}}</ref>
 
Aaron produced several more books and articles, including a book in [[Welsh language|Welsh]] on the history of philosophy, ''Hanes athroniaeth—o [[Descartes]] i [[Hegel]]'' in 1932.<ref name = Jones/> His attempts to boost interest in philosophy in Wales included establishing in that year a philosophy section at the University of Wales Guild of Graduates, which still conducts its proceedings in Welsh.<ref name = Jones/> From 1938 to 1968 he was the editor of the Welsh journal ''[[Efrydiau Athronyddol]]'' ''('Philosophical Studies').''<ref>{{Cite book |last= |first= |url=https://archive.org/details/oxfordcompaniont00meic |title=The Oxford companion to the literature of Wales |date=1986 |publisher=Oxford [Oxfordshire] ; New York : Oxford University Press |others= |isbn=978-0-19-211586-7 |editor-last=Stephens |editor-first=Meic |pages=1 |url-access=registration}}</ref>

Other notable publications of Aaron's include "Two Senses of the Word Universal" (1939)<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Aaron |first=R. I. |date=1939 |title=Two Senses of the Word Universal |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2250857 |journal=Mind |volume=48 |issue=190 |pages=168–185 |issn=0026-4423}}</ref> and "Our Knowledge of Universals", a study read to the [[British Academy]] in 1945 and published in its ''[[Proceedings of the British Academy|Proceedings]]'' and as a separate monograph.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Aaron |first=Richard Ithamar |url=https://archive.org/details/ourknowledgeofun0000aaro |title=Our knowledge of universals |date=1975 |location=New York |publisher=Haskell House Publishers |others= |isbn=978-0-8383-0108-1 |url-access=registration}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Price |first=H. H. |date=1946 |title=Review of Our Knowledge of Universals |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3747701 |journal=Philosophy |volume=21 |issue=79 |pages=187–191 |issn=0031-8191 |url-access=registration}}</ref> Aaron's fascination with the idea of a [[Universal (metaphysics)|universal]] culminated in ''The Theory of Universals'' (1952).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Baylis |first=Charles A. |date=1954 |title=Review of The Theory of Universals |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2020617 |journal=The Journal of Philosophy |volume=51 |issue=14 |pages=417–420 |doi=10.2307/2020617 |issn=0022-362X |url-access=subscription}}</ref> Here, he attacks the notion of universals as [[Platonic realism|Platonic forms]], but is as critical of [[Aristotle's theory of universals|Aristotelian]] realism on [[essences]] as he is of [[nominalism]] and [[conceptualism]] as theories of universals.{{Sfn|Jones|1988|p=384}}

In 1952–1953, Aaron was a visiting professor at [[Yale University]]. In 1956, he was able to study the third draft of Locke's ''[[An Essay Concerning Human Understanding]]'' at the [[Pierpont Morgan Library]], which led to a substantial addition to the second edition of ''John Locke'', published in 1955. He became a [[Fellow of the British Academy]] (FBA) and president of the [[Mind Association]] in the same year. In 1956, the Joint Session of the [[Aristotelian Society]] and Mind Association (publisher of the journal ''[[Mind (journal)|Mind]]'') was held in [[Aberystwyth]], and Aaron gave the inaugural lecture.{{Sfn|Jones|1988|p=386}} In 1957 he was elected President of the Aristotelian Society.<ref name = Jones/>

In 1967, Aaron published a second edition of ''The Theory of Universals'' with a new preface and several additions and rewritten chapters. In 1971, he published a third edition of his Locke biography and the book ''Knowing and the Function of Reason'', which includes broad discussion of the laws of [[Law of noncontradiction|non-contradiction]], [[Law of excluded middle|excluded middle]] and [[Law of identity|identity]], of the use of [[language]] in [[speech]] and [[thought]], and of [[Substance theory|substance]] and [[causality]].<ref name = Jones/>

After retiring in 1969, he taught for a semester at [[Carlton College]], [[Minnesota]], before returning to Wales, where he helped to write articles for the 1974 edition of the ''[[Encyclopædia Britannica]]''.<ref name = Jones/> He began to feel the effects of [[Alzheimer's disease]] and died at his home in [[Aberystwyth]] on 29 March 1987.<ref name = Jones/><ref>{{Cite news |last=Anon. |date=1 April 1987 |title=Professor R. I. Aaron |url=https://archive.org/details/2011Null/Apr%2001%201987%2C%20The%20Times%2C%20%2362731%2C%20UK%20%28en%29/page/n13/mode/1up |work=[[The Times]] |page=14}}</ref>
